sources.title: Margherita Facella, Orontids, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Scholarly dynastic history, updated 2021; Orontid Armenia after Alexander and disputed Armavir letter.

sources.title: James R. Russell, Artaxias I, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Boundary steles, Aramaic titulature and dynasty. The transliteration MLK RWNDKN is printed explicitly, with an alternative reading.

sources.title: Nina Garsoïan, Tigran II, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Reign, territorial expansion, war and the settlement with Pompey in 66 BCE.

sources.title: Cyril Toumanoff, Arsacids vii: The Arsacid dynasty of Armenia
sources.note: Succession, aristocratic institutions and partition; precise Christianization date is disputed, so public text uses early fourth century.

sources.title: Marie Louise Chaumont, Armenia and Iran ii: The pre-Islamic period
sources.note: Long historical sequence; partition is placed around 387 because the article notes alternative dates. No use of speculative ethnogenesis claims.

sources.title: Rüdiger Schmitt, Armenia and Iran iv: Iranian influences in Armenian language
sources.note: Opening discussion of Armenian as an Indo-European language, Iranian influence and fifth-century written attestation.

sources.title: Marta Lorenzon and colleagues, Exploring mudbrick architecture and its re-use in Artaxata, Armenia, during the 1st millennium BC, PLOS ONE (2023)
sources.note: Micromorphology and material characterization at Artaxata. Recycling is the authors’ interpretation; distinguish material remaking from simply reusing intact bricks.

sources.title: Carmen Ting and colleagues, The Artaxiad capital of ceramic: Exploring the changing local pottery production and exchange at Artaxata (Armenia) from the 2nd century BCE to 1st century CE, Archaeological Research in Asia (2023)
sources.note: Publisher-indexed original abstract accessed; direct page failed. DOI 10.1016/j.ara.2023.100444. Its 53-sample analysis and shifts from public to domestic assemblages support the passages.

sources.title: Torben Schreiber, The Archives of Artaxata: Archival Practice in the Capital of Ancient Armenia (2021)
sources.note: Jagiellonian University repository’s indexed original abstract; direct access failed. Distinguishes former private-archive interpretation from proposed public city archive.

sources.title: University of Münster, Easternmost Roman aqueduct discovered in Armenia (2021)
sources.note: Armenian-German excavators’ institutional report; construction attributed to 114 to 117 CE, with wider scientific dating explicitly reported. Underlying paper is Failed Roman Imperialism, DOI 10.34780/8f82-fyw2.

sources.title: University of Münster, Archäologen entdecken älteste Kirche Armeniens (2024)
sources.note: Excavators’ report on an octagonal church at Artaxata, radiocarbon-dated wooden platforms and architectural finds.

sources.title: Roman Provincial Coinage I 3842, University of Oxford
sources.note: Catalogued copper coin, Artaxata; attribution to Tigranes III or V and dating circa 10/5 BCE or circa 6 CE are explicitly uncertain. Greek reverse names Erato as the king’s sister.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Shared regional history across successive dynasties, not an assertion of identical dynastic states. Keep each imported interval: -323 to -200 and -1 to 400. Tigranes’ empire falls in their gap. Imported alias Sasanian E is erroneous and proposed aliases replace it. Boundary mismatch is explicit in public text.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Ancient highland outlines; see ../identities.json. No association with medieval or modern Armenia records.
